patient.name: Terence Doyle
patient.complaint: Breathless walking uphill and a dry cough for 18 months
background: Paroxysmal AF on bisoprolol and apixaban
Retired taxi driver in Bromley; no dust or bird exposure

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older man, progressive exertional breathlessness, a dry cough, clubbing and fine bibasal 'velcro' crackles; or 'most likely cause' with a drug (amiodarone, methotrexate, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin), a job or a hobby in the stem.

points: Breathless walking uphill, now on the flat too.
Tired; no fevers, no weight loss.

steps.lead: Terence is the typical **IPF** patient: an older man (median age 70) who used to smoke.
Terence's stiff lungs fit **interstitial fibrosis**: lower compliance and poorer gas exchange. With no drug, job or autoimmune cause, think **IPF**.

points: Crackles do not change with coughing.
No joint swelling, no rash, no tight skin.

steps.lead: Every IPF feature is here: gradual exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, clubbing and **fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles**.

steps.title: Crackles and cough: fibrosis vs its mimics
head: Feature
Pulmonary fibrosis
Bronchiectasis
Heart failure

steps.q: Terence's fibrosis is at the lung bases. Which cause typically gives upper lobe fibrosis instead?
steps.r: **Silicosis** is in CHARTS (upper lobe). Asbestosis, IPF and RA all cause **lower** lobe fibrosis.

steps.lead: Terence's **basal** fibrosis fits the lower-lobe list (IPF). Upper lobe fibrosis would point you to **CHARTS** causes.
Before calling it idiopathic, check Terence's drugs, job, hobbies and joints. His cardiologist is considering **amiodarone**, a classic cause.

steps.text: Fine bibasal crackles alone do not mean heart failure. **Clubbing** plus a **dry cough** and no raised JVP or oedema means fibrosis.
Farmer with fever, myalgia and dry cough hours after handling **mouldy hay** = **extrinsic allergic alveolitis** (type III hypersensitivity).

investigation.exam: Expect 'most likely finding on spirometry' (restrictive: FEV1/FVC above 0.7, both reduced, low TLCO) and 'most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis' (HRCT). Echo assesses cor pulmonale.

steps.lead: Terence's GP starts with a **chest X-ray** and **spirometry**, plus an autoimmune screen and routine bloods.

visual.title: Terence's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral reticular shadowing at both bases, with small lung volumes.

steps.title: Pulmonary function tests
steps.text: Both volumes fall, so the ratio is preserved: a **restrictive** pattern with low gas transfer.

visual.title: Terence's FEV1/FVC ratio
visual.label: Terence 0.85
visual.caption: A normal or high ratio with low FEV1 and FVC is restriction, not obstruction.

steps.q: Which test will confirm and classify Terence's lung disease?
steps.r: **HRCT** is the gold standard: it shows the pattern and extent. BAL is only for uncertain cases.

steps.lead: Terence's HRCT shows **basal, peripheral honeycombing**: a typical UIP pattern, which fits IPF without needing a biopsy.
Terence's echo is checked for **right heart strain**, because cor pulmonale is the complication of advanced fibrosis.

steps.text: A FEV1/FVC of 0.85 is not 'normal spirometry' when FEV1 and FVC are both below 80%. Read all three numbers.

management.exam: Expect 'most appropriate management': pirfenidone or nintedanib to slow IPF, pulmonary rehab, long-term plus ambulatory oxygen when hypoxic, removing the cause (drug, antigen), and transplant only in a selected subset.

steps.q: Which drug can slow Terence's IPF?
steps.r: **Nintedanib** (or **pirfenidone**) slows progression. Methotrexate can itself cause fibrosis.

steps.lead: Terence is referred for **pulmonary rehabilitation** and started on **nintedanib** to slow the fall in his lung function.
Terence's care is shared with a respiratory specialist, with oxygen if he becomes hypoxic and support for him and his wife.

steps.q: Terence's cardiologist wants to start amiodarone for his AF. What should be done first?
steps.r: A **chest X-ray before amiodarone** checks for pre-existing lung disease. Terence's fibrosis makes amiodarone a poor choice.

visual.title: Terence's FVC (% predicted)
visual.caption: Antifibrotics slow the decline; they do not reverse fibrosis.

steps.lead: If Terence becomes more breathless and hypoxic, it means progression, and he needs **urgent assessment**.

points: Two years on: breathless dressing himself.

steps.lead: At 74 with right heart strain, Terence is not a transplant candidate. He gets **long-term plus ambulatory oxygen**, and low-dose opiates for breathlessness.

steps.title: IPF management pathway
nodes: Confirm on HRCT; remove any cause
Pirfenidone or nintedanib to slow progression

steps.lead: Terence's workup used both guideline points: the **restrictive** definition (ratio above 0.7, both reduced) and the **CHARTS** list to place basal fibrosis.

steps.text: Oral steroids are **not** a treatment for IPF. They help some secondary causes (e.g. hypersensitivity pneumonitis), not idiopathic disease.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with a low TLCO, why the ratio is preserved, how drugs cause fibrosis, or why it leads to cor pulmonale.

steps.title: How fibrosis forms
nodes: Excess collagen and matrix laid down

steps.lead: In Terence's lungs, repeated small injuries heal badly, and **collagen** replaces the alveoli.
Terence's stiff interstitium explains his numbers: low compliance gives **restriction**, a thick barrier gives a low **TLCO**, and both volumes fall together.

steps.q: Why is Terence's FEV1/FVC ratio preserved at 0.85?
o: Both FEV1 and FVC fall together
steps.r: Stiff lungs shrink **both** volumes; the airways are open, and elastic recoil even empties them faster.

steps.lead: The honeycombing on Terence's HRCT is **end-stage** fibrosis: cysts with thick fibrotic walls where alveoli used to be.
Had Terence been given amiodarone, it could have injured his alveolar cells directly or by **hypersensitivity**, adding drug-induced fibrosis.
Terence's swollen ankles came from chronic hypoxia: **pulmonary hypertension** strained his right ventricle, causing **cor pulmonale**.

mcq.q: What is the median age at presentation of IPF?
mcq.r: Median age **70**; more common in men and smokers.

mcq.q: Which crackles are typical of pulmonary fibrosis?
Which is a cause of upper lobe fibrosis (CHARTS)?
mcq.r: **TB** is the T in CHARTS. The others cause lower lobe fibrosis.

mcq.q: Which drug is a classic cause of pulmonary fibrosis?
What is the gold-standard investigation for fibrotic lung disease?
mcq.r: **HRCT** shows the pattern (e.g. basal honeycombing in IPF).

mcq.q: Which spirometry pattern fits pulmonary fibrosis?
mcq.r: **Restrictive**: ratio above 0.7 with FEV1 and FVC below 80%, and low TLCO.

mcq.q: How is extrinsic allergic alveolitis confirmed according to the notes?
mcq.r: **Serum precipitins** to Aspergillus and mould antigens.

mcq.q: Which are the first-line disease-modifying drugs for IPF?
What is first line for end-stage fibrosis with hypoxia?
Why is TLCO reduced in pulmonary fibrosis?
mcq.r: A thickened interstitium **increases the diffusion distance** for gas exchange.

prompts.q: What is fibrotic lung disease, and who typically gets IPF?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: older male ex-smoker with gradual breathlessness = IPF until a cause is found.

points.p: Interstitial lung fibrosis that reduces compliance and impairs gas exchange
IPF is the most common, with a poor prognosis
points.why: Median survival is only a few years.
A young patient points to a secondary cause such as sarcoid or CTD.

points.p: More common in men and smokers
points.why: Classic stem: ex-smoker man in his 70s.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and signs of IPF?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dry cough plus clubbing plus velcro crackles.

points.why: Over months to years, not days.
Not a feature of COPD or heart failure.
Coarse crackles that change with coughing are bronchiectasis.

prompts.q: Which drugs cause pulmonary fibrosis, and what must you do before starting amiodarone?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always scan the drug history in a fibrosis stem.

points.why: First-line DMARD in RA (RA itself also causes ILD).

prompts.q: Which causes give upper lobe fibrosis (CHARTS), and which give lower lobe?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the zone on the X-ray narrows the cause.

points.p: Lower lobe: IPF, RA, asbestosis, SLE, scleroderma, drugs

prompts.q: What is extrinsic allergic alveolitis and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the hobby or job (farmer, birds) is the clue.

points.p: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a type III hypersensitivity reaction
Example: farmer's lung from fungal spores in mouldy hay
points.why: Bird fancier's lung is the other classic.

points.p: Acute: fever, myalgia, dry cough, dyspnoea, bilateral airspace shadowing

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations, and what does spirometry show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ratio above 0.7 but both volumes below 80% = restrictive.

points.p: Chest X-ray: bilateral reticular/reticulonodular shadowing, honeycombing

points.why: Low gas transfer reflects the thick barrier.

prompts.q: What is the gold standard, what does it show in IPF, and how is cor pulmonale assessed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: HRCT to diagnose, echo for the right heart.

points.p: IPF: honeycombing and ground glass, peripheral and basal
Bronchoscopy with BAL in uncertain cases
Echocardiogram for right heart strain (cor pulmonale)

prompts.q: How is IPF treated, from diagnosis to end stage?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: antifibrotics slow, they do not cure.

points.p: Pirfenidone or nintedanib to slow progression
Long-term oxygen plus ambulatory oxygen if hypoxic
Lung transplant in a selected subset
Low-dose opiates or benzodiazepines for symptoms
points.why: Relieve breathlessness at end of life.

prompts.q: How do you manage secondary fibrosis and prevent drug-induced disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: remove the cause first.

points.p: Treat the underlying cause: remove the exposure or treat autoimmune disease
points.why: E.g. rehome the birds, stop the drug.

points.p: CXR before starting amiodarone or nitrofurantoin

prompts.q: Why does fibrosis cause restriction, a low TLCO and a preserved ratio?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: compliance, diffusion distance, proportional fall.

points.p: Repeated epithelial injury and aberrant healing with excess collagen
Thick barrier increases diffusion distance: low TLCO
FEV1 and FVC fall proportionately, so the ratio is preserved

prompts.q: Why does fibrosis lead to cor pulmonale, and how do drugs cause it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hypoxia → pulmonary hypertension → right heart.

points.p: Chronic hypoxaemia causes pulmonary vascular remodelling
Pulmonary hypertension then right heart failure (cor pulmonale)
points.why: Raised JVP, ankle oedema, loud P2.

points.p: Drugs: direct cytotoxic injury to alveolar epithelium and/or hypersensitivity

glossary.IPF: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: progressive scarring of the lung with no identifiable cause.
glossary.ILD: Interstitial lung disease: disorders that inflame or scar the lung interstitium.
glossary.Interstitium: The tissue between the alveoli and capillaries where gas exchange happens.
glossary.Velcro crackles: Fine, end-inspiratory crackles like pulling apart velcro; typical of pulmonary fibrosis.
glossary.Clubbing: Bulbous fingertips with loss of the nail-bed angle; seen in fibrosis, bronchiectasis and lung cancer.
glossary.Compliance: How easily the lungs stretch; low in fibrosis.
glossary.Restrictive pattern: Spirometry with FEV1/FVC above 0.7 but FEV1 and FVC both below 80% predicted.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: Fraction of vital capacity breathed out in one second; preserved or high in restriction.
glossary.TLCO: Transfer factor for carbon monoxide: how well gas crosses into the blood; low in fibrosis.
glossary.TLC: Total lung capacity; reduced in restrictive lung disease.
glossary.HRCT: High-resolution CT: thin-slice CT that shows the pattern of interstitial lung disease.
glossary.Honeycombing: Clustered cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls on HRCT: end-stage fibrosis.
glossary.Ground-glass: Hazy increased lung density on CT through which vessels are still visible.
glossary.UIP: Usual interstitial pneumonia: the basal, peripheral honeycombing CT pattern typical of IPF.
glossary.BAL: Bronchoalveolar lavage: washing a lung segment through a bronchoscope and analysing the fluid.
glossary.Reticular shadowing: A net-like pattern of lines on X-ray from thickened interstitium.
glossary.CHARTS: Mnemonic for upper lobe fibrosis: coal, histiocytosis/HP, ankylosing spondylitis, radiation, TB, silicosis/sarcoid.
glossary.Extrinsic allergic alveolitis: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: immune reaction to inhaled organic antigens such as mouldy hay or bird proteins.
glossary.Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: Another name for extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
glossary.Farmer's lung: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from fungal spores in mouldy hay.
glossary.Serum precipitins: Blood antibodies against specific inhaled antigens; support hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
glossary.Type III hypersensitivity: Immune-complex-mediated reaction, causing inflammation where complexes deposit.
glossary.Pirfenidone: Oral antifibrotic drug that slows IPF progression.
glossary.Nintedanib: Oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor that slows IPF progression.
glossary.Antifibrotic: Drug that slows the laying down of scar tissue.
glossary.Pulmonary rehabilitation: Supervised exercise and education programme to improve breathlessness and function.
glossary.Ambulatory oxygen: Portable oxygen used while walking or active.
glossary.LTOT: Long-term oxygen therapy: oxygen for at least 15 hours a day for chronic hypoxaemia.
glossary.Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
glossary.Pulmonary hypertension: Raised pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
glossary.Amiodarone: Antiarrhythmic drug that can cause pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid and liver problems.
glossary.Bleomycin: Chemotherapy drug, used in testicular cancer, that causes pulmonary fibrosis.
glossary.Methotrexate: Antifolate DMARD used in RA; can cause pneumonitis and fibrosis.
glossary.Nitrofurantoin: Antibiotic for urinary infection; long-term use can cause pulmonary fibrosis.
glossary.Asbestosis: Lower-lobe pulmonary fibrosis from inhaled asbestos fibres.
glossary.Silicosis: Upper-lobe fibrosis from inhaled silica dust; raises TB risk.
glossary.Pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from inhaled mineral dust (coal, silica, asbestos).
glossary.Ankylosing spondylitis: Inflammatory spinal arthritis in young men; can cause apical fibrosis.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has an 18 month history of gradually worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He is an ex-smoker. He takes no regular medicines and worked in an office. His fingers are clubbed and there are fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles. His JVP is not raised and there is no ankle oedema.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: decide fibrosis vs its mimics, then look for a cause.

clues: takes no regular medicines and worked in an office
steps.x: Older male ex-smoker, gradual, dry cough, clubbing, velcro crackles; no drug or job cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No identifiable cause: **idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis**.

elim: Asbestosis needs an asbestos job (builder, shipyard).
Bronchiectasis gives copious sputum and coarse crackles.
No raised JVP or oedema; heart failure does not club.
Sarcoid is younger, with BHL and upper zone change.

steps.x: **D. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.** Rule: old ex-smoker man + dry cough + clubbing + velcro crackles + no cause = IPF.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man has progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He has fine bibasal crackles and clubbing. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows bilateral basal reticular shadowing.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?

steps.x: 'Establish the diagnosis' = the gold-standard test.
Labs: ratio 0.84 with low FVC and TLCO = restrictive. Fibrosis suspected; now confirm and classify.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HRCT chest** shows the pattern (e.g. basal honeycombing).

elim: BAL is only for uncertain cases after HRCT.
Echo assesses cor pulmonale, not the lung diagnosis.
Repeating spirometry delays diagnosis.
Autoantibodies look for a cause but do not confirm fibrosis.

steps.x: **C. High-resolution CT chest.**

technique.stem: A 71 year old woman has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis confirmed by HRCT showing basal subpleural honeycombing. She has no autoimmune disease and takes no drugs that cause fibrosis. Her FVC is 70% of predicted. She has been referred for pulmonary rehabilitation and asks if any medicine can help.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?

steps.x: Drug treatment for confirmed IPF.
Typical IPF; no secondary cause to treat.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pirfenidone** or nintedanib to slow progression.

elim: Azathioprine is not an IPF treatment.
Methotrexate can cause pulmonary fibrosis.
Steroids do not help IPF.
Steroid plus immunosuppressant combinations harm IPF patients.

steps.x: **D. Pirfenidone.** Rule: IPF drug = pirfenidone or nintedanib.

technique.stem: A 76 year old man has advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Over the last 3 months he has developed swollen ankles. His oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air. His JVP is raised, there is a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound and pitting oedema to his knees. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle and a normal left ventricle.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his ankle swelling?
o: Vascular remodelling from chronic hypoxaemia causing pulmonary hypertension

steps.x: Mechanism of oedema in advanced fibrosis.

clues: dilated right ventricle and a normal left ventricle
steps.x: Hypoxia, pulmonary hypertension (loud P2), right heart only.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cor pulmonale**: hypoxaemia → vascular remodelling → pulmonary hypertension → RV failure.

elim: No renal failure given.
The left ventricle is normal.
Mitral stenosis gives a mid-diastolic murmur and AF, not lung fibrosis.
Constriction gives a small, non-dilated heart.

steps.x: **E. Vascular remodelling causing pulmonary hypertension.** Rule: fibrosis + right heart failure = cor pulmonale.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has 9 months of increasing breathlessness and a dry cough. She has taken nitrofurantoin every night for 3 years to prevent recurrent urinary infections. She has never smoked. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are fine bibasal crackles.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Long-term nitrofurantoin is a classic cause of lower-lobe pulmonary fibrosis. IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion, so it is not 'idiopathic' when a causative drug is present.

steps.x: Diagnosis: fibrosis, then check for a cause.
Fibrosis picture in a woman on long-term nitrofurantoin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drug-induced fibrosis** from nitrofurantoin.

elim: No raised JVP, orthopnoea or oedema.
IPF is idiopathic: it needs no identifiable cause.
Aspiration gives recurrent pneumonias, not a gradual dry cough.
Sarcoid is younger, with BHL and upper zone change.

steps.x: **C. Nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary fibrosis.**

practice.stem: A 32 year old man has 2 months of breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He finished chemotherapy for a testicular germ cell tumour 4 months ago. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. There are fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles. His chest X-ray shows bilateral basal reticular shadowing.
practice.q: Which drug is the most likely cause of his lung disease?
practice.e: Bleomycin, used for testicular cancer, causes pulmonary fibrosis. Cisplatin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic; etoposide mainly causes myelosuppression.

steps.x: Most likely cause: a drug.
Fibrosis after testicular cancer chemotherapy; restrictive with low TLCO.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bleomycin** lung.

elim: Cisplatin causes kidney damage and hearing loss.
Etoposide causes myelosuppression.
Ondansetron does not cause fibrosis.
Paracetamol does not cause fibrosis.

steps.x: **A. Bleomycin.** Rule: testicular cancer chemo + fibrosis = bleomycin.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man has progressive breathlessness and a dry cough over 2 years. He has finger clubbing and fine bibasal crackles. HRCT shows peripheral, basal honeycombing. He has pulmonary function tests.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result of his pulmonary function tests?
o: FEV1/FVC 0.78, FEV1 and FVC normal, TLCO normal
practice.e: Fibrosis is restrictive: ratio above 0.7 with a low FVC, and a reduced TLCO from the thickened barrier. A raised TLCO suggests pulmonary haemorrhage, not fibrosis.

steps.x: A finding question: restrictive or obstructive, and the TLCO.

clues: finger clubbing and fine bibasal crackles
steps.x: IPF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ratio above 0.7, FVC below 80%, **TLCO reduced**.

elim: A low ratio is obstruction (COPD).
Mild obstruction with normal TLCO is asthma-like.
Normal results do not fit honeycombing.
TLCO is reduced, not raised, in fibrosis.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: fibrosis = restrictive + low TLCO.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has 18 months of worsening breathlessness and a dry, non-productive cough. He is a retired accountant and an ex-smoker. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 140/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His fingers are clubbed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of his chest?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
Coarse crackles that clear with coughing
Stony dullness and absent breath sounds
practice.e: IPF gives fine, end-inspiratory 'velcro' crackles at both bases. Coarse crackles that change with coughing are bronchiectasis; bronchial breathing is consolidation.

steps.x: Make the diagnosis, then pick its sign.
Older ex-smoker, dry cough, clubbing: IPF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fine bibasal end-inspiratory (velcro) crackles**.

elim: Bronchial breathing is consolidation.
Coarse crackles that change are bronchiectasis.
Polyphonic wheeze is asthma or COPD.
Stony dullness is a pleural effusion.

steps.x: **C. Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles.**

practice.stem: A 48 year old man has had worsening breathlessness for a year. He has had low back pain and morning stiffness since his twenties and an episode of anterior uveitis. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his lung fibrosis?
practice.e: Upper lobe fibrosis with inflammatory back pain and uveitis in a man is ankylosing spondylitis (the A in CHARTS). Asbestosis, IPF, RA and amiodarone cause lower lobe fibrosis.

steps.x: Cause of fibrosis: check the zone first.

clues: low back pain and morning stiffness since his twenties
steps.x: Inflammatory back pain + uveitis = AS; the X-ray shows **upper** zone fibrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper lobe = CHARTS: **ankylosing spondylitis**.

elim: Amiodarone gives lower zone fibrosis, and he is not on it.
Asbestosis is lower lobe with pleural plaques.
IPF is basal and in older patients.
RA causes lower lobe fibrosis.

steps.x: **B. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Rule: upper zone fibrosis = CHARTS.

practice.stem: A 45 year old dairy farmer has had three episodes of fever, aching muscles, a dry cough and breathlessness, each starting about 6 hours after forking mouldy hay in his barn. Each settles within 2 days. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recurrent fever, myalgia and dry cough hours after mouldy hay exposure, with positive precipitins, is farmer's lung, a type III hypersensitivity (extrinsic allergic alveolitis). Pneumonia would not recur with each exposure.

steps.x: Diagnosis; the job and the timing are the key.

clues: about 6 hours after forking mouldy hay
fever, aching muscles, a dry cough
steps.x: Repeated flu-like episodes hours after organic dust; precipitins positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Farmer's lung**: extrinsic allergic alveolitis.

elim: Asthma gives immediate wheeze without fever.
IPF is gradual, older, without fevers.
Pneumonia does not recur with each exposure and settle in 2 days.
Sarcoid gives BHL, not exposure-linked episodes.

steps.x: **B. Extrinsic allergic alveolitis.** Rule: hours after organic dust + fever = EAA.

practice.stem: A 75 year old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has 2 months of increasing ankle swelling. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. His JVP is raised, P2 is loud and there is pitting oedema to mid-shin.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess the cause of his ankle swelling?
practice.e: Hypoxia, raised JVP, loud P2 and oedema in advanced fibrosis suggest cor pulmonale; an echocardiogram assesses right heart strain and pulmonary pressure.

steps.x: Which test for the complication.

clues: JVP is raised, P2 is loud
steps.x: Right heart failure from pulmonary hypertension: cor pulmonale.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Echocardiogram** for right heart strain.

elim: Bronchoscopy does not assess the heart.
CXR will not measure right heart function.
Spirometry tracks the lungs, not the cause of oedema.
Precipitins are for hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

steps.x: **C. Echocardiogram.**

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has 2 years of progressive exertional breathlessness, a dry cough and clubbing. He is an ex-smoker with no relevant occupational or drug exposures. Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles are heard. He has a high-resolution CT scan of the chest.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on HRCT?
practice.e: IPF shows honeycombing with ground-glass change, peripheral and basal predominant (UIP pattern). Pleural plaques suggest asbestos exposure; BHL suggests sarcoidosis.

steps.x: Make the diagnosis, then the HRCT finding.

clues: ex-smoker with no relevant occupational or drug exposures
steps.x: IPF.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Basal, peripheral honeycombing** (UIP).

elim: BHL is sarcoidosis.
Pleural plaques mean asbestos exposure.
Tree-in-bud is small airways infection.
Upper lobe cavitation suggests TB.

steps.x: **A. Basal, subpleural honeycombing.**

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has IPF and has been taking nintedanib for 6 months. She gets breathless walking to the shops. Her resting oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air and does not fall on a 6 minute walk test. She has not had any rehabilitation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Pulmonary rehabilitation is the first-line non-drug treatment for IPF. She does not desaturate, so oxygen is not indicated; steroids do not help IPF.

steps.x: Next step for breathlessness in IPF already on an antifibrotic.

clues: does not fall on a 6 minute walk test
steps.x: Already on the drug; not hypoxic enough for oxygen; no rehab yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pulmonary rehabilitation**.

elim: Fibrosis is not an airway disease.
LTOT needs a much lower PaO2 (below 7.3 kPa).
Transplant is for selected end-stage patients.
Steroids do not help IPF.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary rehabilitation.**

practice.stem: An 81 year old man has end-stage IPF. He is breathless at rest and on minimal exertion. He has ischaemic heart disease and chronic kidney disease. His oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Long-term oxygen therapy with ambulatory oxygen
practice.e: In end-stage fibrosis with chronic hypoxaemia, long-term plus ambulatory oxygen is first line. His age and comorbidities exclude transplant.

steps.x: Management of end-stage hypoxic fibrosis.

clues: ischaemic heart disease and chronic kidney disease
steps.x: Labs: PaO2 6.9 kPa twice, normal PaCO2: chronic type 1 respiratory failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LTOT plus ambulatory oxygen**.

elim: Steroids do not help IPF.
Too old and comorbid for transplant.
NIV is for hypercapnia; his CO2 is normal.
Switching antifibrotic will not treat hypoxia.

steps.x: **B. Long-term oxygen with ambulatory oxygen.**

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has had a year of breathlessness and a dry cough. He has kept racing pigeons in a loft at home for 30 years. HRCT shows upper zone fibrosis with ground-glass change. Serum precipitins to avian proteins are positive. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, removing the antigen is central; without it, any treatment fails. Antifibrotics are not the first step here.

steps.x: Initial management of a secondary fibrosis.

clues: Serum precipitins to avian proteins are positive
steps.x: Chronic bird fancier's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Remove the trigger**: avoid the pigeons.

elim: Inhaled steroids are not a treatment for hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Antifibrotics do not remove the cause.
This is not infection.
Not an airway disease.

steps.x: **A. Avoid exposure.** Rule: secondary fibrosis = treat the cause first.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. His haemoglobin is normal. His oxygen saturation is 95% at rest but falls to 85% after climbing one flight of stairs. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his reduced TLCO?
o: Air trapping from small airway narrowing
Destruction of alveolar walls in emphysema
Increased diffusion distance across a thickened interstitium
practice.e: Fibrosis thickens the interstitium, increasing the diffusion distance between alveolus and capillary, so gas transfer falls, especially on exertion when transit time is short.

steps.x: Mechanism of low gas transfer in fibrosis.
Fibrosis; anaemia excluded; desaturation on exertion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thick barrier = **increased diffusion distance**.

elim: Air trapping is obstructive disease.
His haemoglobin is normal.
Emphysema is obstructive, not restrictive.
Nothing suggests PE.

steps.x: **D. Increased diffusion distance.**
